paragraphs: New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez filed a civil lawsuit Wednesday against Jeffrey Epstein's longtime attorney, Darren Indyke, and longtime accountant, Richard Kahn, according to The Guardian. The complaint, filed in federal court in New Mexico, accuses them of having "facilitated and concealed" Epstein's crimes. It names the two men individually and as co-executors of Epstein's estate, and it also names the estate and the 1953 Trust, which holds the estate's assets.

The complaint alleges Epstein, with help from associates, trafficked and abused survivors at locations including his Zorro Ranch in Stanley, New Mexico. It alleges those associates received generous salaries, access to elite social circles and gifts, including being named beneficiaries of his estate. It further alleges that from 2011 to 2019 Indyke received more than $16 million from Epstein and related entities, and Kahn more than $10 million. The state asks the court to bar the men from receiving estate payments while the case proceeds.

In a statement, an attorney for Indyke spoke for both men, saying they "emphatically reject" the allegations that they were complicit in or knowingly facilitated Epstein's abuse. The statement said no woman has accused them of committing or witnessing abuse, and that the attorney general's office did not seek to speak with them before filing. Earlier this year, the pair told a U.S. House committee they had no knowledge of Epstein's crimes during their employment.
Torrez said Epstein "did not operate alone." Several survivors signed a letter backing the suit, and one, Anouska De Georgiou, spoke at a news conference.

The suit comes amid a separate dispute. Torrez sued the Justice Department in August, saying it resisted giving the state unredacted Epstein files. The department has moved to dismiss, arguing that information-sharing decisions are within its discretion and that releasing the files would violate victims' privacy. That case is ongoing.

Thousands of California state workers began a one-day strike on Wednesday, with rallies planned outside government buildings in several cities, according to The Guardian. The walkout is by members of SEIU Local 1000, a union that represents roughly 100,000 public employees, including nurses and teachers. It follows a contract dispute with the administration of Governor Gavin Newsom. Wednesday's picketing was the first of its kind for the union.

The union has been at an impasse with the state since its contract expired on 30 June. Its negotiators say state officials rejected their key proposals: a 20% salary increase over three years, higher state contributions to healthcare, and flexible telework. Newsom has required state workers to be in the office four days a week.

Anica Walls, the union's president, said in a statement that the Newsom administration "can and must do better" and should return to the table and bargain in good faith toward a contract that lets workers afford groceries, childcare and rent. The union has also filed a complaint with California's public employment relations board alleging bad faith bargaining. It claims the state waited until 30 June to respond to some proposals and said there was "no money" for additional compensation.

The state has not commented publicly on the status of the talks, citing confidentiality. California's department of human resources, known as CalHR, had reportedly tried to block the strike, arguing that the union lacked plans to exempt essential workers and was compromising public health and safety. According to the union, the labor board determined a list of about 5,000 workers deemed essential, who will report to work during the strike.
A CalHR spokesperson said in a Wednesday statement that the department "remains focused on achieving a fair and responsible agreement" and remains available at the bargaining table.

Officials in Toledo, Ohio, are investigating a tank explosion that released a chemical into the air and led to a mass evacuation, The Guardian reported. An employee at MC Tank Terminal, a company that transports and stores bulk liquid chemicals, called first responders late Tuesday night. One first responder was taken to the hospital with injuries officials believe are not life-threatening. The cause of the explosion is not yet known.

The chemical released was glycidyl methacrylate, an industrial coating product used in plastics, rubbers and resins. Local officials say the airborne irritant can cause burning of the eyes, nose, mouth and skin. They have advised residents with serious symptoms, such as difficulty breathing, nausea and vomiting, dizziness or confusion, to go to an emergency room or call 911.

Mayor Wade Kapszukiewicz said at a Wednesday news conference that residents within a one-mile radius needed to evacuate, while those within three miles were asked to shelter in place with windows sealed. The city had issued an initial order Tuesday night for about 300 people within a half mile, later expanded to a full mile, covering about 1,000 people. Officials said that as far as they knew, all residents had been evacuated. Local news outlets reported a dense fog over the area and a plastic-like odor.

Kapszukiewicz said the chemical became a gas in the explosion but will turn back into a liquid when it settles in the tank. He said the hope is that the risk of explosion will then have passed and that efforts can begin to contain and eliminate the hazard. Officials said they were unsure how long the evacuation and shelter orders would last. Some schools closed Wednesday and others delayed opening, according to NBC News. Executives from MC Tank Terminal were traveling to Toledo to assess the situation, the mayor said.

Prosecutors in New Taipei, Taiwan, have charged five men over a plot to ram a car into the comedian Huang Yi-hao, who has made fun of the Chinese Communist party and Xi Jinping, The Guardian reported. Prosecutors said Wednesday that an individual from mainland China identified only as "K" paid the five defendants to injure Huang badly enough to require hospitalization. China's Taiwan Affairs Office did not respond to requests for comment.

According to prosecutors and Taiwan's Central News Agency, a GPS tracker was allegedly placed on Huang's scooter months before the attack to learn his daily routines. On 11 September, two defendants drove into his bike as he rode home but stopped after hearing him scream. Huang suffered a bruised pelvis. The suspects then allegedly pretended to help with an insurance claim so they could send a photo of his medical certificate to K. The statement said K refused to pay the full NT$450,000 promised, about US$13,900, because the injuries were only minor.

Prosecutors said the case involves a suspected use of "cross-border suppression tactics" by the Chinese Communist party to direct people in Taiwan to suppress dissenting voices through violence. Taiwan has repeatedly accused China of transnational repression. Beijing claims the island as its territory. In May, two people were prosecuted for spreading feces and paint at a Taipei club hours before a Huang show.

Lev Nachman, a political scientist at National Taiwan University, said this is an extreme case but that threats and violence against critics of the Communist party have occurred in Taiwan for years. Taiwan's Mainland Affairs Council said in October that at least 126 people had been affected by Chinese transnational repression.
Huang said on Facebook he would not cancel future performances but was "no hero." "I write it because it's funny," he said.

A Tunisian military court has sentenced opposition leader Olfa Hamdi to four years in prison on charges of plotting against state security and inciting the military to disobey orders, her lawyer, Akram Moussa, said Wednesday, according to Al Jazeera. Hamdi holds both Tunisian and U.S. citizenship. Moussa said the charges stemmed from social media posts.

The sentence is made up of two separate two-year terms from two additional convictions, plus fines of 80,000 dinars, about $26,000, her lawyer said. Hamdi was also sentenced in March, in a separate case, to two years in prison. Global human rights organizations have widely criticized the cases against her.

Hamdi leads the Third Republic Party and has repeatedly criticized President Kais Saied's rule, calling for a transitional government and early presidential elections. She tried to run for president in 2024, when she was 36, but her candidacy was rejected because she did not meet the 40-year age minimum. She had been living abroad and running a consulting firm in the United States after briefly heading the national airline Tunisair. She was detained at Tunisia's main airport in February after getting off a flight.

A U.S. State Department spokesperson told AFP that Washington was "closely tracking the situation." The spokesperson added that the Trump administration has "no higher priority than the safety and security of American citizens."

Critics describe the case as the latest in a crackdown on Saied's opponents, and rights groups accuse him of rolling back freedoms since a 2021 power grab. Opposition leaders, activists and journalists have been imprisoned during his rule. Saied rejects the accusations, saying the law applies to everyone regardless of position. On Saturday, thousands of Tunisians joined the largest protest against him in years, accusing him of undermining democracy and mishandling the economy.

Airbnb has updated its house rules policy to bar hosts from asking guests to "complete tasks that require significant effort or time, or would typically be performed by a cleaner," The Verge reported. The change applies to reservations booked on or after November 20 and was announced to hosts by email on Wednesday, according to Wired.

Airbnb gave examples. Hosts cannot ask guests to wash and put away dishes, but can ask them to put used dishes in the sink. They cannot ask guests to strip beds or start laundry, but can ask them to gather used towels. They cannot require guests to take garbage off-site, but can ask them to sort trash and recycling into indoor bins. Exceptions include asking guests to use animal-proof trash containers in bear country or take short showers where drought restrictions apply. Airbnb spokesperson Simon Letouze told Wired that hosts can still make "reasonable" requests.

Airbnb will show requests in a new "rules and requests" section, and listings that keep chore requests may display an "includes cleaning requests" warning. Hosts also cannot add rules in messages or on signs. On November 20 Airbnb will also ban requiring guests to sign separate contracts, with limited exceptions such as local legal requirements or an optional amenity like a golf cart rental. Hosts who violate the policies may receive warnings, lose listings or be banned.

Many hosts objected on Airbnb's forum, Reddit and Facebook. One said hosts are asked to accept risks while their ability to protect themselves is limited, and some said the limits pose health risks. Some suggested raising prices, stripping kitchens down, or organizing a strike in which hosts unlist properties for a day or two. Guests, by contrast, were largely celebrating, Wired reported. Airbnb did not immediately say whether hosts' workarounds, such as moving rules to other listing sections, would be allowed.

Missiles struck Kyiv on Wednesday night, hours after Russia said it was "ready in principle" to resume peace talks, the BBC reported. Kyiv Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said several houses were hit and six people were injured.

The attack came during a new US diplomatic push led by President Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. Witkoff met Russian President Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg on Wednesday, a day after meeting Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky in Oslo. Trump said the world was "maybe now the closest we've been" to settling the war.

Putin's aide Yuri Ushakov said a new round of talks could be held around 10 November in Abu Dhabi and must focus on "building a security system for Russia and Ukraine after the end of the conflict." He said the ideas Witkoff brought were not very "useful," and that Putin told Witkoff Russian troops were advancing everywhere. Ukraine and its European allies dispute that, pointing to a virtual stalemate. Witkoff called the talks "constructive."
Zelensky told Fox News he would accept a freeze along the current front line, with security guarantees to be discussed afterward. Three-way talks were paused in February.

Tensions between Washington and Kyiv are growing. Trump has said Ukraine should get a new president and has blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries for rising fuel prices. He also drew criticism from Democratic and some Republican lawmakers after lifting sanctions to let Russia sell diesel; Zelensky and European allies criticized the move too.
Before the talks, Russia released Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old American sentenced to nearly seven years for allegedly fighting for Ukraine. Trump said "there was no 'swap' necessary."

Tesla reported third-quarter results on Wednesday showing roughly flat revenue and sharply lower profit. CNBC said the results beat analyst estimates, and the stock was little changed in extended trading.

The two outlets give somewhat different comparisons. TechCrunch put revenue at $28.04 billion, against $28.09 billion a year earlier. CNBC cited a year-earlier figure of $28.24 billion. Both reported net income of $787 million. TechCrunch described a 43% drop from $1.37 billion, while CNBC said net income attributable to common shareholders fell 29% from $1.11 billion.

Automotive revenue declined 3% to $20.56 billion, according to CNBC. Tesla blamed lower average selling prices and trouble securing batteries. Energy revenue fell 16% to about $2.9 billion, which TechCrunch said Tesla attributed to tariff-related customer refunds. Services and other revenue rose 33% to $4.6 billion.
Spending on Optimus humanoid robots and other AI work weighed on profit. CNBC said capital expenditures more than doubled to $3.73 billion and free cash flow fell 62% to $1.53 billion.

Tesla said it has started Optimus production at its Fremont, California factory. Elon Musk called it "early production," expected a "somewhat bumpy" ramp, and said Tesla could make 20,000 per week by the end of 2027. He said there is still work to do on the AI before the robot is useful for open-ended tasks.
Musk also said the boards of Tesla and SpaceX have formed special committees to discuss a possible merger, which would need shareholder support.

Meta said Wednesday, alongside its third-quarter earnings report, that it will issue a new class of non-voting shares, according to The Verge. Trading is set to begin in 2027. The company said the stock will help fund its artificial intelligence initiatives, as well as potential acquisitions and employee compensation.

In its press release, Meta said the scale of investment needed to compete and expand infrastructure during the AI transformation "is significant." Chief financial officer Susan Li said on the earnings call that the new shares will "expand our funding tools and give us flexibility to invest behind the unprecedented momentum we're seeing."

Meta has spent heavily on AI, building large data centers, hiring talent from rivals such as OpenAI and developing models meant to compete with other tech giants. The company now expects capital expenditures of $135 billion to $145 billion this year, up from its previous estimate range of $130 billion to $145 billion.

The announcement follows a busy period for the company. Meta launched an AI agent called Muse in September. The agent can clean out an email inbox, book restaurant reservations and plan trips. The Verge reported that the Muse app reached the top of app stores and hit 10 million US downloads this week. Meta also rolled out a Muse Wonder model this week.

The launch has had problems. A tech YouTuber reported that the agent gave his address to a stranger on Facebook Marketplace, and Meta paused Muse's conversation-sharing feature after researchers found chats publicly available on the web.

IBM reported third-quarter results on Wednesday that beat analyst expectations, and its shares slipped in extended trading, CNBC reported. Revenue grew about 5% from a year ago. Net income was $2.19 billion, or $2.30 per share, up from $1.74 billion, or $1.84 per share.
CEO Arvind Krishna said in a statement that clients "are now deploying 'Super Intelligence' in ways that transform entire operating models, instead of simply addressing narrow or novel problems."

By segment, software revenue was $7.80 billion, up 8% and above the $7.66 billion analyst consensus. Infrastructure revenue was $3.70 billion, up 4% and above the $3.57 billion consensus. Consulting revenue was $5.34 billion, flat and just below the $5.37 billion consensus. The consulting unit's gross margin narrowed to 27.4% from 28.9% in the second quarter. IBM's adjusted gross margin of 58.5% was below the 59.1% consensus.

Finance chief Jim Kavanaugh said AI accounted for about 30% of consulting revenue in the quarter and 35% of its backlog. He said IBM reinvested productivity gains into digital assets as it moves toward a "services as software model."

IBM raised its outlook for full-year free cash flow growth to more than $1 billion, from about $1 billion in July. It still expects 2026 constant-currency revenue growth of 4% to 5%. Kavanaugh said the company is comfortable with the Street's estimate of about $32 billion in revenue for the year.
During the quarter IBM agreed to buy HRL Laboratories, owned by Boeing and General Motors, for an undisclosed sum. IBM stock is down 15% this year, while the S&P 500 is up 13%.

President Trump was set to travel to South Carolina on Wednesday for a rally with Sen. Darline Graham, Al Jazeera reported. She is the sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, who died unexpectedly in July. The race has grown closer than Republicans expected in a state Trump carried by 18 points in 2024.

South Carolina's governor appointed Darline Graham to finish her brother's term. Trump then endorsed her in a new Republican primary, which she won. He said the endorsement was "in honour of her brother." Her Democratic opponent, pediatrician Annie Andrews, has pointed to Graham's inexperience and her debate performance, including a moment when Graham said she was "not that informed on national security." Graham has called Andrews "the most radical liberal that's ever run for state office in South Carolina." A Real Clear Politics average shows Graham leading by about 2.7 points.

The visit follows an executive order from Trump waiving most sanctions and tariffs on Russia that were established under a law named after Lindsey Graham. Darline Graham told the Associated Press she would "put the pressure on Russia to end the war and get gas prices down" and said she does not trust Putin.
Al Jazeera said Trump enters the final stretch with the lowest approval ratings of his career, as voters voice concern about affordability and the effects of the war with Iran.

It also pointed to other competitive races. In Kansas, polls suggest Republican Ashley Hinson and Democrat Joshua Turek are effectively tied. In Texas, polling averages show Republican Ken Paxton trailing Democrat Talarico by 1.7 points.

Voters prefer a Democrat for Congress by a double-digit margin less than two weeks before Election Day, according to a Strength In Numbers/Verasight poll shared with NPR. Among registered voters the split is 52% to 41%, and among likely voters 54% to 42%. The survey of 2,028 respondents ran Oct. 13-19 and has a margin of sampling error of 2.2 percentage points.

President Trump's job approval stands at 34%, with 62% disapproving and 50% strongly disapproving. G. Elliott Morris, who runs the Strength In Numbers newsletter and Wave Polling and Research, said Trump's ratings hit new lows on seven of 10 tracked issues and that he is now underwater on every issue the poll asks about.

Prices and inflation were named as one of the top three problems by 63% of respondents, and 39% listed it first. Asked which party they trust on their own top issue, voters chose Democrats 47% to 35%, the widest gap the poll has measured. On immigration, Republicans led by an average of 15 points in May 2025, while Democrats now hold a one-point edge. Republicans keep only slim advantages on crime and public safety and on border security.

The poll also frames the midterms as a referendum on Trump. Some 58% said it is more important to elect a Congress that checks Trump, versus 25% who want one that helps pass his agenda. Majorities want Congress to roll back or check his positions on tariffs, health care, immigration and several other areas.

Nearly one in 10 who said they voted in 2024 regret their choice, including almost 15% of self-described Trump voters. NPR said the results help explain why both parties are spending heavily in races in conservative territory.

A federal judge in Tennessee has refused to let the Environmental Protection Agency unilaterally dismiss a Clean Air Act lawsuit over Elon Musk's Colossus data center in Memphis, Ars Technica reported. US District Judge Debra Brown ruled Tuesday that "nothing" in the law lets the EPA Administrator "unilaterally dismiss a citizen suit."

The NAACP sued after unpermitted gas turbines were found powering the data center, which is operated by xAI, now known as SpaceXAI after a merger. The group seeks an injunction requiring the best available pollution control technology and penalties of up to $124,426 per day per violation. It argues the turbines risk raising pollution in nearby, predominantly Black neighborhoods.

The Trump administration intervened, arguing that the EPA can dismiss such suits when the president decides against enforcing the law. According to Ars Technica, it said allowing large civil penalties against AI firms racing to get data centers running would "not serve the public interest," citing the president's AI Action Plan.

Brown called the EPA's reading an "extraordinary position" without grounding in federal law. She said the Clean Air Act's exception for dismissal applies when the government is itself suing or acting to require compliance, and the administration has not said it will sue SpaceXAI. She noted the law also lets citizens sue the EPA Administrator for failing to enforce it, writing that Congress "contemplated that citizen suits may not always align with the EPA's judgment." She also observed that Congress considered, but did not adopt, a 1990 amendment that would have let the EPA take over such suits.
Laura Thoms of Earthjustice, which is working with the NAACP, praised the ruling and said the group will keep pressing the case. Ars Technica did not report a response from the EPA or SpaceXAI.

Iran says it will not give up its enriched uranium, according to Al Jazeera, as a flurry of diplomatic meetings coincides with fears that the war with the United States and Israel could flare again. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, said late Tuesday after meeting Pakistan's army chief Asim Munir: "Not a single gram of enriched uranium will be removed from Iran." He did not rule out downblending the highly enriched uranium inside the country under monitors' supervision, something Iran has offered before.

Parliament speaker and chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf told Munir that Iran had "nothing new" to tell Washington. He said Iran expects conditions offered in New York last month to lead to the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz within seven days. Mediators did not publicly detail their proposals, but were told the US must build trust by accepting Iran's conditions. These include returning to the June memorandum of understanding and recognizing an Iran-Oman deal on temporary transit through the strait.

On the US side, President Donald Trump has said since the war began that he wants to dismantle Iran's nuclear programme. Vice President JD Vance suggested earlier this month that a "meaningful" reduction in enrichment capacity might satisfy US demands. Before the June 2025 attacks, the IAEA estimated Iran held 440 kilograms of uranium enriched up to 60 percent. The agency has been unable to inspect key sites, so the stockpile's current size and location are unverified. Iran says it is not pursuing a bomb.

Analyst Ellie Geranmayeh of the European Council on Foreign Relations said Iran is willing to negotiate over the uranium and monitor access, but only with a clear protocol for sanctions relief, and that the sides are "very far" from that. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said the country is in war conditions. US media, citing unnamed officials, reported the Pentagon is sending a carrier strike group and a Marine unit to the Middle East, which would give Trump strike options after the November 3 midterm elections.

Federal prosecutors in Mexico have charged César Jáuregui Moreno, a former attorney general of Chihuahua state, with treason. They accuse him of allowing US agents to join an April raid on a suspected drug lab without proper authorization. Mexico's Attorney General Ernestina Godoy said he let foreign agents carry out activities reserved for Mexican authorities and failed to share information. Jáuregui, who served from 2023 to this year, has denied the allegations.

The case traces to April 19, when a convoy returning from an operation against suspected methamphetamine labs in a remote, mountainous area plunged into a ravine. Two Chihuahua state investigators and two US agents died. US media reported the Americans worked for the CIA. At the time, Jáuregui said they were embassy "instructor officers" doing training, and in a later statement said they had been present for a drone training session and asked to ride in the convoy back to the airport. He resigned later that month.

Under Mexican law, the federal government must approve the activities of foreign forces on Mexican soil. President Claudia Sheinbaum said after the crash that the military did not know non-Mexicans were taking part, and she called for an investigation. She has declined US-led counter-narcotics operations, even as President Donald Trump pressures Mexico over drug trafficking and has suggested possible unilateral US military action.

Jáuregui, a member of the conservative opposition PAN party, was arrested at the weekend. A judge has ordered pretrial detention while the court decides whether there is enough evidence to proceed, and a hearing is set for Saturday. He also faces state charges, including abuse of public office, and has denied instructing or consenting to US involvement. Experts told Al Jazeera the treason charge is vaguely defined in Mexican law, and an Eurasia Group analyst told Reuters it seeks to set a precedent against state-US cooperation without federal approval.

Cuba has accused the United States of threatening countries with tariffs, visa restrictions and other retaliation to change their votes on an upcoming UN General Assembly resolution calling for an end to the US embargo. Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez made the claim on Wednesday, saying Secretary of State Marco Rubio and UN Ambassador Mike Waltz were personally leading a campaign he alleged had run for months. The vote is expected on October 27 or 28.

Rodriguez said US officials had threatened to suspend cooperation programs, deny visas to officials and their families, and even back opposition parties in upcoming elections. He also said countries were urged to abstain or skip the vote. He called it "a new and dangerous way of conducting multilateral diplomacy." Al Jazeera said it asked the State Department and the US Mission to the UN for comment and had not received a reply by publication.

Waltz did acknowledge lobbying. In a Monday briefing he said Washington had asked European colleagues whether they could keep backing a resolution he called a "propaganda tool for the Cuban regime," citing Ukrainian allegations that Cubans fighting for Russia were not being paid and that the money went to Cuba's government. He also accused Cuban diplomats of harassing participants at a US-hosted panel on alleged human rights abuses in Cuba. Cuba's UN ambassador and other representatives had confronted him as he left the event.

The resolution is nonbinding. The General Assembly has overwhelmingly backed such resolutions almost every year since 1992. The Trump administration says Cuba's government, not the embargo, is to blame for the island's economic troubles, and it has called for regime change. Since the start of 2026, Al Jazeera reports, Washington has blocked oil supplies to Cuba and threatened tariffs on countries supplying fuel, worsening shortages and blackouts.

Pope Leo XIV does not need further treatment after surgery to remove a cancerous growth from his lung, his doctors said in a statement shared by the Vatican. Tests on tissue removed during the operation confirmed a lung adenocarcinoma, as initially diagnosed, and showed the disease was localized. The statement said a later oncological assessment found that "no further treatment is necessary."

The 71-year-old pope had the operation on October 13 at Rome's Gemelli Hospital. It lasted 90 minutes and included removal of the lower lobe of his right lung. He announced the procedure himself during his Sunday prayers, telling people in St Peter's Square that doctors had found a nodule on his lung, which he said was caught "at an early stage."

He was discharged over the weekend, four days after the surgery, stopping to speak to well-wishers as he left the grounds. On Wednesday he held his first weekly general audience since leaving the hospital, at St Peter's Square.

While recovering, he remained active. Images released on Friday showed him celebrating Mass from the hospital in green vestments, standing behind a makeshift altar. The same day the Vatican said he spoke by phone with Russian President Vladimir Putin, urging a ceasefire in the blockaded, Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky so food aid could be delivered, and calling for "dialogue and peace." On Monday he had a similar call with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. People close to the pope have said he was keen not to delay a trip to Latin America planned for early November.

Nigeria's first confirmed Ebola case since the outbreak in East Africa began in May is the wife of a diplomat who traveled to Uganda's capital, Kampala, for a holiday, according to Dr Jean Kaseya, head of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention. Nigeria's health minister, Muhammad Ali Pate, told the BBC the 42-year-old woman spent two and a half weeks in Kampala and had a two-hour stopover in Ethiopia's capital on her return. She is originally from Uganda but based in Abuja.

She arrived home on October 3 and fell ill three days later, Kaseya said. She first sought care at a private hospital, thinking she had malaria, then went to a second, where she was admitted on the 11th. Authorities were alerted on October 19, and the diagnosis was confirmed the next day after three lab tests. Pate said she is stable and improving, and that 44 contacts have been identified. They are in isolation, and none is known to have developed symptoms.

Accounts differ on her movements. Uganda's health ministry earlier described her as a Nigerian national who went to eastern DR Congo for business and only transited through Uganda, adding that Uganda has no confirmed active cases and her passage did not mean she caught the virus there. Pate and Kaseya's comments contradict that, though both played down tension and said officials are working with Uganda, Ethiopia and the Africa CDC to establish the facts.

The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo species, for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment, has killed at least 4,600 people in DR Congo, according to the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control. Kenya has reported at least nine cases. Kaseya urged Western countries not to impose travel restrictions. Pate cited Nigeria's 2014 containment of Ebola and said the country must stay vigilant.

Flapping Airplanes, a year-old AI startup, announced on Wednesday that it raised a $1 billion Series A round, co-led by Index and Lux, reportedly at a $6 billion valuation. The round comes nine months after a $180 million seed round from GV, Sequoia and Index that valued the company at $1.5 billion, so the valuation has roughly quadrupled. Earlier backers Sequoia, GV and Kleiner Perkins also took part, and Nvidia is among its investors.

The company was founded by Aidan Smith and brothers Asher and Ben Spector. Its mission is to find ways to train large models with less data. The founders describe their work as a "megakernel framework" that can run training and inference together on the same chip so it is rarely idle. They say this can build intelligent systems "without ingesting half the internet." Asher Spector told TechCrunch that a model a million times more data efficient would be "a million times easier to put into the economy."

Separately, legal AI startup Legora announced a $550 million Series E at an $8.8 billion valuation, led by Atreides Management with Baron Capital, Bessemer Venture Partners, General Catalyst, Menlo and others. TechCrunch reports the company said its annual recurring revenue now exceeds $200 million, up from $100 million when it announced a Series D extension in April at a $5.6 billion valuation.

The raise comes a month after rival Harvey announced a $550 million round at a $15.5 billion valuation. Harvey said in March that its annual recurring revenue was more than $200 million. Legora plans to use the new capital to expand across North America.

Two AI agent announcements landed on Wednesday. Anthropic launched Claude Duet, an agent for professionals and small business owners, as a research preview, and Meta said on its third-quarter earnings call that its Muse AI app has more than 10 million users, confirming estimates released earlier this week by Sensor Tower.

According to The Verge, Claude Duet is built around Claude Opus 5.5 and is available as a standalone iOS and Android app and through Claude on the web. Anthropic says it sends a morning brief on key items across connected apps, messages users during the day only when something needs attention, and can take on tasks from scheduling meetings to building dashboards and forecasts. It asks for approval before big steps such as sending a payment or deleting something, and uses a new classifier and safety prompt meant to reject requests to share the strictest tier of information, such as credit card numbers. Anthropic calls it an "early version" that might misread a thread or miscalibrate urgency, and says it is not as strong at personal errands like booking tickets. Access is by waitlist, and users must be Pro or Max subscribers in the US.

On the Meta call, CEO Mark Zuckerberg said about 25 percent of people who set up Muse now use it daily. Over a quarter of engaged users shopping through the agent had an average purchase above $200. Other popular uses include connecting it to email or calendars.

Zuckerberg said Meta will now focus on scaling Muse, raising revenue and cutting compute costs, which he expects to improve more than tenfold in the next year. Meta plans to keep Muse free for most users, take a share of commerce on the platform, and charge power users. He also described a future "Muse network" in which users' agents work with friends' and families' agents.

Walmart will let customers use AI agents to shop on its website starting next month, announced Wednesday by the retailer. The company said CEO John Furner discussed the plans at the Masters of Scale Summit in San Francisco. The move contrasts with Amazon, which has blocked Perplexity's shopping agent and Meta's Muse AI assistant from making purchases for shoppers, according to The Verge and TechCrunch.

At the center is an "Agent Gateway," currently in beta, which connects approved agents to Walmart through the Model Context Protocol, an open standard for linking agents to outside services. Walmart says it lets agents search its online inventory and buy on a user's behalf without browser hiccups. It also says the gateway helps an agent find a customer's usual items, such as a favorite brand of milk, without sharing the customer's broader shopping history. Shopping through agents will also work at Sam's Club, and a Walmart+ membership is not required.

Customers will authorize each agent through an "Agent Profile" on their account. By default, every agent purchase needs approval, but shoppers can set a spending limit, such as $100. Purchases appear separately from the customer's own, and a profile can be deleted at any time. Walmart compares the controls to adding an authorized user on a credit card.

Walmart has also published terms for agents. They must not take actions beyond what the shopper intends, cannot change payment methods or access payment information, and may access only the information needed for a task. Agents that break the terms will be blocked. Walmart says its returns process applies even when an agent does not act as intended. It has previously announced a partnership with Meta's Muse and offers integrations with apps such as ChatGPT and Gemini.

Recursive, an AI startup founded last year, released its first model, Flint, on Wednesday. It is a free coding model that can run on a laptop, and the company says it was built largely with the help of AI. Recursive credits its automated research system, the Eureka Machine, with helping on nearly every step, including pre-training, post-training and inference. That let a small team build the model from scratch in under four months, according to TechCrunch.

Flint is a mixture-of-experts model that uses 2.5 billion of its 40 billion parameters at a time. It is free to download on Hugging Face under the Apache 2.0 license. In Recursive's tests it generated about 131 tokens per second on a MacBook Pro with an M4 Pro chip, roughly double comparable models. On SWE-Bench Verified it outperformed other models under 50 billion parameters. Only Alibaba's Qwen3.8 27B scored higher on Recursive's own six-test average. The company acknowledged Flint needs more guidance than large paid coding assistants.

Wired's Will Knight, who tested Flint on a Mac with 48GB of memory, said it handled his coding requests every time, including a to-do list app and a research-scouring tool. Recursive says Eureka's contributions include a sparser model shape, low-bit training that shrank Flint by 71 percent with almost no quality loss, and custom kernels.

The approach is debated. Some experts worry that AI improving itself could escape human control, and Wired reports several bills in Congress propose banning it. Recursive CEO Richard Socher calls such fears more science fiction than reality. He says Flint was built with a system that cannot escape human control, and that the goal is full recursive self-improvement overseen by humans who could stop it. Recursive has raised $650 million at a $4.65 billion valuation.

General Motors unveiled a new fourth-generation EV platform on Wednesday at its annual GM Forward event in New York, and the announcement focused on computing and software rather than traditional vehicle engineering. According to TechCrunch, GM described new battery chemistries, revamped electric motors, and a new central computing platform and electrical architecture connecting systems from braking and steering to software.

The new Central Compute Unit is 40 times more powerful than GM's existing systems, the company says. It will handle propulsion and chassis controls as well as perception and active safety. Eliminating smaller chips at the vehicle's edges should trim wiring by 30 percent. GM says the unit will also work in gasoline models. It will debut in 2028 on the Cadillac Escalade IQ, which TechCrunch describes as the automaker's technological flagship.

GM also said it will roll out an autonomous highway driving feature in 2028 that lets drivers take their hands and eyes off the road without needing to be ready to take over. Product chief Sterling Anderson told TechCrunch he wants vehicles to become spaces that "understand context" and "reduce friction."

The push comes as automakers face pressure from Tesla and Chinese manufacturers, which have shortened development cycles to two to three years from the usual four to five. GM says it wants to cut its own timeline in half, and gave one example: engineers went through 300,000 virtual designs of a new lithium-manganese-rich battery pack before building a physical prototype. GM's capitalized software amortization expense in 2025 was $866 million. TechCrunch notes that Volkswagen struggled with its own software effort and struck a $5.8 billion joint venture with Rivian.
